title: Content (Philippians 4:11–13)
hook: I have learned to be content, and I can do all things in him

segments.voice: Yesterday, whatsoever things are true, lovely and of good fame. Your line was think on these. What good thing did you dwell on? Day five hundred ninety-one.

I can do all things. You've seen it on gym shirts, on locker-room walls, under an athlete's eyes in black grease paint. It's usually read as a promise of winning: with God's help I'll make the team, close the deal, run the marathon. Read in place, it's something quieter. It comes near the end of a thank-you note. The church at Philippi had sent Paul a gift in prison, carried by a friend named Epaphroditus. And Paul, thanking them, says something surprising about needing it.
screen: `I CAN DO ALL THINGS: ON A GYM SHIRT.` → `READ IN PLACE: A THANK-YOU NOTE.` → `A GIFT SENT TO A PRISONER.`

segments.voice: He's glad of the gift, but he doesn't want them to think he was desperate: "Not as it were for want. For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Then he names the states. He knows how to be brought low and how to abound; to be full and to be hungry; to have plenty and to go without. And he says he's been instructed in all of it. The Greek word is the one used for being initiated into a secret. Paul has learned the secret of being content. Then: "I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me." All things, here, means both: hunger and plenty, prison and freedom. Not winning, but standing steady through either. The word for content is autarkēs, and it's borrowed. It was a favorite ideal of the Stoic and Cynic philosophers: self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul takes their word and changes its center. Not sufficient in myself, but sufficient in him. And notice the first verb: I have learned. Contentment, for Paul, isn't a personality type. It's a skill, and it took practice, and he learned it in some very hard places. Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment speaks of the same freedom: a heart that isn't ruled by envy or by the need for more, which the Catechism calls poverty of heart. And Paul doesn't despise the gift either. He calls it a sweet fragrance, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Content doesn't mean ungrateful. It means grateful, without being owned.
screen: `NOT AS IT WERE FOR WANT.` · `BROUGHT LOW, AND ABOUNDING.` · `AUTARKĒS: SUFFICIENT, BUT IN HIM.` · `CONTENTMENT IS LEARNED.` · then, large: `I CAN DO ALL THINGS IN HIM WHO STRENGTHENETH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take inventory of now. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are and name, quietly, five things that are here. A chair holding you up. Light. Your breath. A sound. A person, or the memory of one. Don't name what's missing. Just what's here. Let it be enough for these two minutes. If a want shows up, notice it and let it pass by. If you pray, you can say today's verse slowly. If you don't, simply rest in what's already here. The bell holds the time.
Content. Paul's word from prison: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content, because I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Today's word.
Your line: I have learned. Today, when you feel the pull of wanting more, name one thing that's already enough. Day five hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment commends "poverty of heart" and freedom from envy and greed; many Catholics practice contentment through simplicity, fasting and almsgiving.

original.note: Greek: self-sufficient, content; a Stoic ideal that Paul re-centers 'in him' (Philippians 4:11).

trapdoor: what you thought: God will help me win.
what it means: Paul has learned to be steady in hunger and in plenty, through Christ who strengthens him.
what a scholar hears: autarkēs, the Stoics' word, re-centered; memuēmai, 'I've been initiated' into the secret.
